frames.narration: A flaw in a library lets an attacker run code on the search service. Search legitimately talks to one thing: the cache. On the flat network, though, that is not all it is allowed to do.

Flat network: the attacker scans and connects to the orders service and the orders database directly. 11 hosts, including all 3 crown jewels (orders database, users database, payments), are within reach.

Segmentation: hosts are grouped into edge, app, data and ops zones, and only the needed zone-to-zone connections are allowed. Search is in the app zone, which may reach the data zone, so the databases are still reachable. The radius shrinks from 11 to 7 hosts on a direct hop, but the crown jewels remain.

Identity-based access: every service has a certificate and each callee lists who may call it. The orders database accepts only the orders service. Search presents its own certificate, which is not on that list.

The blast radius from search is now one host, the cache it really uses. Summed over all 12 possible entry points, the takeovers that are possible fall from 132 on the flat network to 41. A host such as the web front end still pivots through the services it is meant to call, so least privilege and per-request checks still matter.
Now the extreme. A policy that lists only reviewed flows breaks 4 of the 23 flows the system needs, because nobody updated it for new calls.

To stop the outage, each broken flow gets an exception that lets the caller reach a whole zone. Search can now reach all 3 hosts in the data zone, including a database it never needed. The policy works again, but it has 8 connections nobody needs and nobody remembers why.
